intro: Look around your room. A lamp has a switch and a light. A pet has a name and can eat and play. Each thing keeps some information about itself and knows how to do some actions. **Object-oriented programming**, or **OOP**, builds programs the same way: the program is a team of small [[objects|a bundle of data plus the actions that work on that data]] that keep their own information and ask each other to do things.

Almost every app you use is written this way: games, banks, shops, phone apps. Big programs are hard to change without breaking something. OOP gives programmers tools to decide **where each piece of knowledge lives**, so that a change in one place does not break ten others. That is the real goal of every idea in this summary.

You will learn what classes and objects are, how objects hide their insides (encapsulation), how one class can build on another (inheritance), how the same call can do different things (polymorphism), what interfaces and abstract classes are for, why we often prefer building with parts instead of inheriting, how to spot messy code, what happens when things go wrong (exceptions), how to write code that works for many types (generics), how memory is cleaned, how to read and write data, and how other languages do OOP without classes. Most examples use Java, the language of the quiz. At the end you will be ready to answer it.

sections.title: The big picture: objects talking to objects

blocks.text: Think of a school. The teacher does not open the student's backpack and look inside. She **asks**: 'please show me your homework'. The student decides how to find it. In OOP, objects work like this. One object sends a request, called a **method call**, and the other object decides how to answer.

rows: An object keeps its data private and offers only safe actions.
A vending machine: you press buttons, you cannot reach inside.
We show what an object can do and hide how it does it.
You drive a car with a wheel and pedals, without knowing the engine.
A new class starts from an old one and adds or changes things.
A puppy is a dog, and a dog is an animal.
One request, many answers, depending on the object.
'Make a sound' makes a dog bark and a cat meow.
An object is built from other objects.
A bike has wheels, a chain and a bell.
blocks.caption: The five ideas of the summary

blocks.text: The goal of OOP is not to use fancy words. The goal is to put every rule in one place, so that changing it later is cheap.

blocks.title: Curso de POO Java, Gustavo Guanabara (in Portuguese)

blocks.text: A cookie cutter is not a cookie. It is the **shape** used to make many cookies. A **class** is the cutter: it says which data (called **fields**) every thing of this kind has and which actions (called **methods**) it can do. An **object** is one cookie made from it, also called an **instance**. Two accounts made from the same `Account` class have the same methods, but each one has its own balance.

blocks.caption: A class and two objects

blocks.text: Constructors, this and static

items: A **constructor** sets up a new object. It has the same name as the class and no return type.
If you write no constructor, the compiler adds one with no arguments. As soon as you write any constructor, that free one disappears.
`this.x` means 'the field x of this object'. It helps when a parameter has the same name as the field.
`this(...)` calls another constructor of the same class. It must be the first line of the constructor.
A `static` field belongs to the class, not to an object. There is one copy for everybody, like the number on a school bell. A normal (instance) field exists once per object.

blocks.text: Order of construction

When `new` runs, Java first runs the constructor of the superclass (the class above, see inheritance). Then it runs the field initialisers and the `{ }` initialisation blocks, **in the order they are written in the file**. Only at the end does the rest of the constructor body run. An `int` field that copies another field copies the value at that moment and stays unlinked afterwards.
Access levels

rows: Classes in the same package (folder of classes)
blocks.caption: Java access levels, from the most closed to the most open. Use the most closed one that works.

blocks.text: Passing objects and comparing them

Java passes **everything by value**. For an object, the value that is copied is the **reference**, like a paper with the address of a house. If a method uses the address to paint the door, the owner sees the new color. But if the method writes a new address on its own copy of the paper, the owner's paper does not change. In short: changing the object through a parameter is visible to the caller, reassigning the parameter is not.

`==` on two object variables asks 'is it the very same object?' (identity). `equals` is meant to ask 'do they have the same contents?', but the version inherited from `Object` also compares identity. A class must override `equals` (and `hashCode`) to compare fields. A Java `record` writes them for you.
Encapsulation

**Encapsulation** means the data of an object can only be reached through the methods of its own class. Then the class can protect its **invariants**, rules that must always be true, such as 'a balance is never negative'. It can also change how it stores things without breaking its users.

A `private` field is only the start. If a getter returns the internal `List`, outsiders change it without passing through your rules. Return a copy (`List.copyOf`), a read-only view (`Collections.unmodifiableList`), or offer the operations instead. The same is true for immutable classes: `final` fixes the reference, not the object it points to, so also copy mutable things on the way in (defensive copy).

**Tell, don't ask.** Do not ask the cashier for the money in the till and then decide for her. Tell her 'take this payment' and let her apply the rules. In code: instead of reading the balance, comparing it outside and writing it back, call `account.withdraw(amount)` and let the account decide.
Class = the shape, object = one thing made from it. Rules about the data live inside the class.

sections.title: Life of an object: memory and garbage collection

blocks.text: Imagine your desk and a big storage room. Small notes stay on the desk and are thrown away when you leave. Bigger things go to the storage room. In Java, the desk is the **stack**: local variables and parameters live in the box of each method call and vanish when it returns. The storage room is the **heap**: every object made with `new` lives there. A variable like `Point p` holds only a **reference** (an address) to the object on the heap.

blocks.caption: The variable p is on the stack, the object is on the heap

blocks.text: Who throws away objects nobody uses? In C++ with manual management, you write `delete` yourself. Forget it and you have a **leak**. Delete too early and you have a **dangling pointer**. Java gives this job to the **garbage collector** (GC).
What is garbage?

An object is garbage when the program has no way to reach it. The GC starts from the **roots** (local variables on the stacks and static fields), follows every reference, and marks what it reaches. What is not marked can be freed. This is **tracing**, or mark and sweep. Reachability is **transitive**: an object only pointed to by unreachable objects is unreachable too.

blocks.content:
root a ──► [1] ──► [2] ──► [3]

after  a.next = null :
root a ──► [1]        [2] ──► [3]   (2 and 3 are garbage)
blocks.caption: Setting null cuts a reference. 3 is still pointed to, but only by garbage

items: Assigning `null` removes only that one reference. If another path reaches the object, it stays alive.

**Reference counting** frees an object when its counter hits zero, but it cannot see cycles (A points to B and B points to A). Tracing, used by the JVM, handles cycles: if nobody reachable points to the pair, both are freed.
Being eligible does not mean being collected right now. The virtual machine decides when.

blocks.text: Generations and leaks

Most objects die young (a temporary result, a loop variable) and the ones that survive tend to live long. This is the **generational hypothesis**. So the heap is split: new objects are born in a small young area (eden) that is cleaned often, survivors are promoted to the old generation, cleaned rarely.

A GC frees only what is unreachable. It cannot know what you will never use again. A static list that only grows keeps everything alive, and the server ends with `OutOfMemoryError`. Fix it by removing entries, limiting the size (a cache with eviction) or using weak references.
Memory is for the GC. Files, sockets and locks are not: close them yourself with `finally` or try-with-resources, never with `finalize` (deprecated since Java 9, slow and unreliable).

sections.title: Inheritance: a class that builds on another

blocks.text: A puppy is a dog, and a dog is an animal. Everything true for animals is true for dogs, and dogs add their own tricks. **Inheritance** does this in code: `class Manager extends Employee` makes `Manager` a **subclass** of `Employee` (the **superclass**). It receives the members of the superclass and may add or change behaviour. Because it keeps every promise of the superclass, a `Manager` can be used wherever an `Employee` is expected. The opposite is false.

blocks.caption: A class tree. Every Java class has one direct superclass; the root is Object

items: Java allows **one** superclass only (single inheritance). This avoids getting two versions of one method by two paths. To fulfil many contracts, a class `implements` several interfaces.
`Object` is the root and gives every class `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode`.
A subclass object contains the fields of the whole chain. A `private` field of the superclass exists in it, but only the superclass methods can touch it. That keeps the superclass invariants safe.
`final` on a variable forbids reassignment, on a method forbids overriding, on a class forbids inheriting (like `String`).

blocks.text: Constructors in a chain

Every constructor begins by calling another: `this(...)` or `super(...)`. If you write neither, the compiler inserts `super()`. If the superclass has only constructors with parameters, that hidden call cannot work and the code does not compile: the subclass must call `super(args)` explicitly. So construction climbs up to `Object`, and the bodies run from the most general class to the most specific.

blocks.content:
new C()  where C extends B extends A

A body runs first  ->  B body  ->  C body
blocks.caption: Bodies run from top to bottom of the tree

blocks.text: Overriding rules

To **override** a method, the subclass repeats its signature with a new body. It may offer more than the superclass, never less: the access can stay the same or widen (`protected` to `public`), the return type can be a subtype, and the checked exceptions cannot be broader. This way any code written for the superclass still works.
Casting up and down

An **upcast** (`Animal a = new Cat()`) is implicit and always safe. A **downcast** (`(Dog) a`) must be written and is checked while running against the real class of the object: if `a` holds a `Cat`, it throws `ClassCastException`. Test first with `instanceof`, which in modern Java also declares the new variable: `if (a instanceof Dog d)`.

Two traps. (1) A field with the same name in the subclass does not override the superclass field, it only **hides** it. The object has two fields, and the one used depends on the declared type of the variable, decided at compile time. Avoid it. (2) A superclass constructor that calls a method the subclass overrides will run the subclass code before the subclass fields are set, so it sees default values (`0`, `null`). Constructors should not call overridable methods.
Inheritance is for 'is-a' where the subclass keeps every promise of the superclass. Constructors run from the top down.

Say 'make a sound' to a room with a dog, a cat and a cow. Each one answers in its own way, and you did not need to know which animal it was. That is **polymorphism**, 'many forms'. In code, we write against a general type (a superclass or an interface), for example `rule.apply(total)`, and every object runs its own version. New kinds can be added without changing the caller.
Two types for one variable

In `Shape s = new Circle();` the variable has a **declared (static) type**, `Shape`, and the object has a **real (dynamic) type**, `Circle`. The compiler uses the declared type to check that the call is allowed. The virtual machine uses the real type to pick the code. Choosing at run time is **dynamic dispatch** (also late binding). It is usually done with a per-class table of methods, called a vtable.

blocks.content:
s.area()
  declared type Shape  -> compiler: does area() exist? yes
  real type Circle     -> run time: use Circle's area()

search starts at the real class and climbs:
Puppy -> Dog -> Animal -> Object
blocks.caption: Two steps for one call

blocks.text: If a subclass does not override the method, the search climbs and finds the nearest superclass version. Objects of the superclass itself keep the original. Inside an override, `super.draw()` calls the version of the direct superclass of the class where it is written, with no dynamic dispatch. It lets you extend instead of replace.
Overloading is not overriding

rows: Same name, different parameters, same class
Same signature, new body in a subclass
At compile time, by the declared types of the arguments
At run time, by the real class of the receiver

blocks.text: Java does **single dispatch**: at run time only the class of the object that receives the call counts, never the classes of the arguments. If you pass a `String` stored in an `Object` variable, the compiler picks `print(Object)` and it stays that way. When behaviour must depend on both objects, programmers use **double dispatch** (the Visitor pattern).

`static` methods are not polymorphic. `p.name()` is just `Parent.name()`, chosen by the declared type, and the object is not even looked at. A static method with the same signature in the subclass hides the other. Also, `equals(Coin c)` does not override `equals(Object o)`, it adds a second method, and collections call the `Object` one. Write `@Override`: the compiler then rejects the typo.
Why it matters: killing the if chains

If the same decision by type (`if role == DEVELOPER ... else if role == DBA ...`) is repeated in many methods, every new role means editing all of them, and forgetting one is easy. With polymorphism, each role is a class that implements a common interface and carries its own rules. Old code does not change: **open for extension, closed for modification** (the open-closed principle).
Example of rules in a list, applied in order, each starting from the result of the previous one: a price of 10000 cents, then 10% off, then 500 off, then 10% off again.

blocks.title: Price in cents after each discount rule

blocks.text: Compiler checks with the declared type, the virtual machine runs the code of the real type. Order matters when rules are chained.

A wall socket does not care if you plug in a lamp or a toaster. It only defines the shape of the plug. An **interface** is the plug: it lists the method signatures that can be asked of an object, and the classes that `implement` it supply the code. Code written against the interface works with any implementation, present or future.

An **abstract class** is a recipe with a missing step. It can have fields, constructors and finished methods, but leaves one or more methods without a body, marked `abstract`. Because part of it is missing, you cannot create an object directly from it. The first concrete subclass must give a body to every inherited abstract method.

rows: How many a class can use
A role that unrelated types can play
Sharing state and code among close relatives

blocks.text: Default methods and the diamond

Once, adding a method to an interface broke every class that implemented it. A `default` method brings a body that classes inherit, so `forEach` could enter the Java 8 collections without breaking old code. But a class may then receive two defaults with the same signature. Java settles it with three rules:

items: A method from a **class** always beats one from an interface (the 'class wins' rule). So a `default` can never change a class that already had that method, and cannot redefine `toString` or `equals`.
A more specific interface beats the one it extends.
If there is still a tie, the class does not compile until it overrides the method itself.

blocks.text: Template Method

The abstract class can fix the order of the steps in a `final` method that subclasses cannot change, and leave some steps abstract or overridable. The subclass fills the gaps, and the overall order stays guaranteed by the superclass. This is the **Template Method** pattern.

blocks.caption: The recipe is fixed, one step is open

blocks.text: Two design principles

items: **Dependency inversion**: business rules and details should both depend on abstractions. If `Checkout` does `new SaoPauloTax()` inside, it is glued to that class. Receive a `Tax` interface through the constructor (**constructor injection**) and it can use any tax.

**Interface segregation**: prefer small interfaces, one per role. A wide `Document` interface (read, write, delete) forces a read-only class to throw `UnsupportedOperationException`, which breaks whoever trusts the contract. Split it, and let methods ask for the narrowest type they need (`Readable` for a `preview`).

blocks.text: Interface = a role, no state, many allowed. Abstract class = shared state and code, only one. Class wins over interface defaults.

There are two ways to reuse a class. **Inheritance** says 'is a': a dog is an animal. **Composition** says 'has a': a car has an engine. A car cannot be used where an engine is expected, so `Car extends Engine` is wrong. The deciding question is **can one be used in place of the other?** If yes, inheritance can be considered. If not, hold the other object in a field and delegate work to it.

blocks.caption: Composition and delegation

blocks.text: Aggregation and composition in UML

Both are whole-part links. In **aggregation** (hollow diamond) the part has its own life and may belong to several wholes: a team and its athletes. In **composition** (filled diamond) the part belongs to one whole, which creates and destroys it: a building and its flats, an order and its lines. Which one you choose depends on the system's requirements.
Why 'prefer composition over inheritance'

items: **Strongest coupling.** A subclass depends on how the superclass is written, not only on what it promises. With composition, you only use the public interface and can even swap the object while running.

**Fragile base class.** A `CountingBag` that overrides `add` and `addAll` can count items twice if the superclass `addAll` itself calls `add`. That internal detail is not in the contract and may change. If the counter instead holds a bag and delegates, the inner calls never come back to it.

**Too much inherited.** `Stack extends ArrayList` also inherits `add(0, x)` and `remove`, so a client can break the last-in-first-out rule. With composition the class exposes only `push` and `pop`. The real `java.util.Stack` (extends `Vector`) has this flaw.

**Behaviour fixed at birth.** Inheritance decides behaviour when the object is created. With composition, the varying part lives in another object behind an interface, and putting a different object in the field changes behaviour while running. It also avoids a subclass explosion when there are several axes (shipping and tax).

blocks.text: The Liskov substitution principle

A program written for the base type must stay correct with **any** subtype. In maths every square is a rectangle. But if `Rectangle` has `setWidth` and `setHeight`, a mutable `Square` that changes both sides breaks the user who sets 5 by 4 and expects area 20. So 'is-a' in inheritance is about **behaviour**, not about how things are classified in the real world.

rows: Be equal or weaker: accept at least as much
Base accepts any positive amount, subclass refuses amounts above 1000
Be equal or stronger: promise at least as much
Base guarantees a non-negative result, subclass may return a negative one
blocks.caption: Ask for no more, deliver no less

blocks.text: Use inheritance only for a true subtype that you can substitute. For reuse alone, use composition.

A good toolbox keeps hammers with hammers and screws with screws. That is **cohesion**: the parts of a class work towards one goal. A cohesive class has one reason to change (the single responsibility principle), is small and easy to name and test. A sign of low cohesion is a class whose methods use different sets of fields.

**Coupling** is how much one class depends on others, like wires between boxes. You cannot remove it, since objects must work together, but you can choose it: depend on few things, and on stable ones such as interfaces. The classic goal is **high cohesion and low coupling**.

items: **Afferent coupling**: how many classes depend on me. If it is high, I carry a lot of responsibility and changing my public interface is risky.
**Efferent coupling**: how many classes I depend on. If it is high, I have many outside reasons to change.
A class used by 20 others and using none is the riskiest one to change in its interface. Point dependencies toward stable modules.

blocks.text: Code smells

A **code smell** is a pattern that suggests code is hard to understand or change. The program works and the tests pass, but the next change will be slow. **Refactoring** means changing the structure without changing the behaviour, and the proof is that the same tests pass before and after.

rows: 40 lines in blocks separated by comments
Extract Method: each block becomes a named method
One class validates, computes, e-mails and reports; hard to test
Extract Class: one per responsibility, the old one coordinates
A method uses only getters of another class
Move Method to the class that owns the data (tell, don't ask)
One change needs edits in many places (switches for payment methods)
Gather them: an interface with one class per method
Strings and ints for e-mail, tax number, money; swapped arguments compile
Small types (value objects) that validate in the constructor
Conditional chain on a type code
Same `if` chain by kind in many methods
blocks.caption: Six smells from the catalogue of this repository

blocks.text: For this repository's measurement, adding a fourth kind of delivery to a checkout:

blocks.title: Existing files edited to add one new kind

blocks.text: The trade is not free: with polymorphism, a new kind is one new class, but a new operation on all kinds edits the interface and every class. Choose by what changes more often.
Cyclomatic complexity

It counts the independent paths through a method, so it hints at how many tests you need. In the quiz, **start at 1 and add 1 for every `for`, `if`, ternary `?:`, `&&` and `||`**. A method with one `if` and one `for` has complexity 3. High values suggest extracting methods or using polymorphism.
High cohesion, low coupling. A smell is a hint, not a bug. Refactor with the same tests green.

In a relay race, if a runner drops the baton, she shouts and the team stops its normal plan until someone knows what to do. An **exception** is that shout. Throwing it interrupts the normal flow, and the virtual machine **unwinds the call stack** method by method, looking for a `catch` that matches. If it reaches the top without finding one, the thread ends and the error is printed. This lets a low-level method detect a problem and a higher level, which knows what to do, handle it, with no return codes passed hand to hand.

blocks.content:
main()  ── has catch (IOException)
  └ load()
      └ read()   <- throws IOException here

search: read -> load -> main (found!)
blocks.caption: The exception travels up until a catch matches

blocks.text: Checked and unchecked

Everything thrown descends from `Throwable`. **Checked** exceptions (for example `IOException`) are failures that can happen even in a correct program, like a missing file. The compiler forces you to handle them or declare them with `throws`. **Unchecked** ones (`RuntimeException` and its children, such as `NullPointerException`) usually show a bug, and `Error` is a serious failure of the machine. The compiler does not force you to catch them.
try, catch, finally

items: When a statement in `try` throws, the rest of the `try` is skipped. Control goes to the first matching `catch`, then to `finally`, and then the program continues after the whole structure. There is no way back to the failing line.

The `catch` blocks are tried in order and the first whose type equals the exception or is a superclass wins. So put the most specific first. Putting a superclass before its subclass does not compile, because the second block would be dead code.
`finally` runs however control leaves the `try`: normal end, `return`, caught or uncaught exception. It does not run only if the machine stops (for example `System.exit`).

blocks.caption: The return value is set aside before finally runs

blocks.text: A `return` inside `finally` replaces the saved value and also hides exceptions. Never do it.
Try-with-resources

For files and connections, write `try (Res a = ...; Res b = ...)`. Objects that implement `AutoCloseable` are closed for you when the block ends, with or without an exception. They are closed in the **reverse order** of opening, like a stack, because a later resource may use an earlier one.
Translate, but keep the cause

Each layer should speak its own language: whoever calls `place(order)` does not need to know SQL, so you catch `SQLException` and throw `OrderNotSavedException`. The new exception must carry the original as its **cause**: `new OrderNotSavedException(msg, e)`. This is **exception chaining**; the printed trace shows both, joined by `Caused by`. Without it, the diagnosis is lost.
Specific catch first, finally always runs, close resources with try-with-resources, always chain the cause.

Labeled boxes are better than mystery boxes. A `List<String>` is a list labeled 'strings only'. The compiler rejects `add(42)` and knows that `get(0)` returns a `String`. Without the label, everything is an `Object`, and every read needs a cast that may fail while running. **Generics** let you write a class or method once and use it with many types, still checked.
The main collections

rows: Waiting line, one or both ends
Unique keys, each with one value
blocks.caption: Choose the interface by the contract, then the implementation by cost and order

blocks.text: In a `Map`, `put` with a new key adds an entry. With a key already there, it replaces the value and returns the old one, so the size counts distinct keys. `TreeSet` sorts by natural order (`Comparable`) or by a `Comparator`.
Rules of the Java generics

items: **Only reference types.** `List<int>` does not compile. Use the wrapper `Integer` (and `Double`, `Boolean`). The compiler converts in both directions (**autoboxing** and **unboxing**), at the cost of one object per element.
**Invariance.** `Integer` is a subtype of `Number`, but `List<Integer>` is **not** a `List<Number>`. If it were, you could add a `3.14` into a list of integers.
**Bounds.** An unbounded `T` only has the methods of `Object`. `T extends Comparable<T>` unlocks `compareTo`, so `max(a, b)` works for any type that compares with its own kind.

**Wildcards.** `? extends T` for things you only read from (a producer). `? super T` for things you only write to (a consumer). Memory aid **PECS**: producer extends, consumer super. Copying from `List<Integer>` to `List<Number>` uses `copy(List<? super T> dst, List<? extends T> src)`.

**Type erasure.** After checking, the compiler replaces `T` by its bound (or `Object`) and inserts casts. The compiled code does not know what `T` was. So `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` have the same class at run time, and you cannot write `new T()`, `new T[10]` or `x instanceof List<String>`.

blocks.text: Fail-fast iterators

Collections of `java.util` count their modifications. If you remove from a list inside a for-each loop, the iterator notices and throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. The name is misleading: no second thread is needed. To remove while looping, use the iterator's own `remove()` or `removeIf`.
Generics = checking at compile time, erased at run time. PECS for wildcards. Never change a collection inside its own for-each.

A stream is a garden hose: data flows in one direction, and you take it piece by piece. A **byte stream** (`InputStream`, `OutputStream`) moves raw 8-bit numbers with no meaning. A **character stream** (`Reader`, `Writer`) adds the **encoding**, the rule that turns bytes into letters. Using the wrong kind on text corrupts accented letters.

Byte and character are the same only for plain ASCII. **UTF-8** is variable length: the first 128 characters take 1 byte, an accented letter such as `ç` takes 2, the euro sign 3, an emoji 4. To count bytes of a text, add the size of each character (the word `ação` has 4 characters but 6 bytes). Read text with a character stream and **state the encoding**, or you will cut accented letters in half.

blocks.title: Bytes of one character in UTF-8

blocks.text: Buffers

Going to the operating system for every single character is like walking to the library for each word. A **buffered** stream (`BufferedReader`) brings a whole page at once and hands out letters from memory. Writing is similar, with one warning: data reaches the destination only when the buffer fills, or on `flush()` or `close()`.
Serialisation

An object in memory is a web of references that only makes sense inside the running program. To save it in a file or send it over a network, you **serialise** it: turn its state into a line of bytes (Java binary, with `ObjectOutputStream`) or text (JSON, XML). A Java class opts in by implementing the marker interface `Serializable`.

items: `transient` leaves a field out: use it for passwords, caches, connections. When the object is read back, it is rebuilt without calling the constructor of the serialisable class, and transient fields come back as `null`, `0` or `false`.

The stream also stores the class name and a version number. On reading it compares with the loaded class. If you changed the class and declared no `serialVersionUID`, the computed number changes and reading old files throws `InvalidClassException`. Declaring `private static final long serialVersionUID` lets the class evolve compatibly.

blocks.text: Binary serialisation ties the file to the shape of the class. For data that lives long, explicit formats such as JSON are usually safer.
Bytes for raw data, characters for text with an encoding, buffer for speed, `transient` and `serialVersionUID` for serialisation.

sections.title: OOP across languages: traits, interfaces, protocols

blocks.text: Not every language has classes and inheritance like Java. But they all need ways to group data and behaviour and to let different things answer the same request. Here is how some do it.

rows: Nominal interfaces: a class must declare `implements`
Structural interfaces: matching members are enough
Structural interfaces, no classes, no inheritance
Traits on structs and enums, static (`T: Display`) or dynamic (`dyn Trait`)
blocks.caption: Same need, different tools

blocks.text: Nominal against structural

In a **nominal** system (Java), a value belongs to a type because its class says so by name. In a **structural** system (TypeScript, Go), having the needed members is enough. A `Book` with a `price` fits `Priced` in TypeScript without saying `implements`, and a plain object `{ price: 5 }` fits too, which is handy for test doubles. The same class without `implements` is refused in Java.

blocks.caption: Structural typing in TypeScript

blocks.text: Nominal typing records intent and avoids coincidences (two `run` methods that mean different things). Structural typing gives flexibility and needs no adapters for types you do not own. In Go, a small interface can be defined on the consumer side, and an existing type, even from another library, satisfies it unchanged.
The expression problem

Objects group code **by variant** (one class per kind). Adding a kind is easy, adding an operation means editing every class. Functions with pattern matching group code **by operation**. Adding an operation is easy, adding a kind means editing every function. This repository measured it: adding 'take and pay' to a cart was one new file with objects, and four edits inside one file with functions. The opposite change has the opposite cost.
Ask which direction your design will grow. And in the functional style, use a compiler with exhaustiveness checking, so it points at every case you forgot.
Nominal = declared by name. Structural = enough to have the members. Traits and protocols give polymorphism without class inheritance.
All the tools of OOP answer one question: where does each piece of knowledge live, and how does a change spread? Use this table when you meet a quiz question.

rows: Rules live next to the data
Each kind carries its own rules
Subclass breaks when the parent changes
The format is coupled to the class
Memory grows forever with a GC
Declared type for overloads, real type for overrides

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: Believing that `private` is enough while a getter returns the internal list.
Mixing up overloading (compile time) and overriding (run time), and forgetting that static methods and fields are not overridden.
Using inheritance only to reuse code, or because 'a square is a rectangle'.
Calling an overridable method from a constructor.
Catching a superclass exception before its subclass, or throwing a new exception without the cause.
Thinking `List<Integer>` is a `List<Number>`, or that the type `T` still exists at run time.
Trusting the garbage collector to close files.

blocks.text: Good OOP is a way to make future changes small. High cohesion, low coupling, depend on abstractions, and prefer composition unless the subtype really substitutes.
